why_use_this: This is the linear-algebra foundation nearly every other numeric package in the vani-* ecosystem builds on -- [vani-algebra](https://github.com/enthusiasticgeek/vani-algebra)'s eigenvalue-based root finder, [vani-pde](https://github.com/enthusiasticgeek/vani-pde)'s elliptic solvers, [vani-optimize](https://github.com/enthusiasticgeek/vani-optimize)'s Newton-step machinery, and [vani-tensor](https://github.com/enthusiasticgeek/vani-tensor)'s contraction all call into this package rather than reimplementing linear algebra themselves. Reach for it directly whenever your problem is naturally a matrix: solving a linear system \( Ax=b \), finding a determinant/inverse/eigenvalue, or just doing matrix arithmetic. Matrices are flat row-major `Vec<f64>` with explicit dimension arguments -- no hidden metadata, no `Matrix` struct -- so a matrix from this package is byte-for-byte interchangeable with a rank-2 [vani-tensor](https://github.com/enthusiasticgeek/vani-tensor) tensor. For small fixed sizes (2x2, 3x3) there are direct closed-form functions that avoid the overhead and numerical cost of the general n×n path; use those when you know your size in advance.

math_notes.dot_n: \( x \cdot y = \sum_{i=1}^n x_i y_i \) -- the standard vector dot product (named `dot_n` rather than `dot` to avoid colliding with the compiler's own builtin `vec_dot`).
math_notes.vec_outer: \( (x \otimes y)_{ij} = x_i y_j \) -- the outer product, an \( m \times n \) rank-1 matrix from an \( m \)-vector and an \( n \)-vector.
math_notes.mat_norm_fro: \( \lVert A \rVert_F = \sqrt{\sum_{i,j} A_{ij}^2} \) -- the Frobenius norm, the matrix analog of the vector L2 norm (treats the matrix as one long vector of entries).
math_notes.mat_norm_max: \( \max_{i,j} |A_{ij}| \) -- the largest absolute entry, the max-norm.
math_notes.mat_mul: \( C = AB \) for square \( n\times n \) matrices: \( C_{ij} = \sum_{k=1}^n A_{ik}B_{kj} \), the standard triple-loop matrix product.
math_notes.mat_mul_rect: \( C = AB \) for rectangular \( A \) (\( m\times k \)) and \( B \) (\( k\times n \)), giving an \( m\times n \) result: \( C_{ij} = \sum_{l=1}^k A_{il}B_{lj} \) -- the general (non-square) form `mat_mul` specializes and [vani-tensor](https://github.com/enthusiasticgeek/vani-tensor)'s `tensor_contract_last_first` reuses directly.
math_notes.mat_vec_mul: \( y = Ax \): \( y_i = \sum_{j=1}^n A_{ij}x_j \) -- matrix-vector product, the \( n=1 \)-column special case of `mat_mul_rect`.
math_notes.mat_pow_n: \( A^p \) for a non-negative integer \( p \), via exponentiation by repeated squaring (\( O(\log p) \) matrix multiplications instead of \( p-1 \)): accumulate the result from \( A^{2^k} \) for each set bit \( k \) of \( p \)'s binary representation.
math_notes.mat_inv_2x2: \( \begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{ad-bc}\begin{pmatrix}d&-b\\-c&a\end{pmatrix} \) -- the direct closed-form adjugate-over-determinant formula, undefined when the determinant is 0.
math_notes.mat_det_3x3: The 3x3 determinant via cofactor expansion along the first row: \( \det A = a(ei-fh) - b(di-fg) + c(dh-eg) \) for \( A = \begin{pmatrix}a&b&c\\d&e&f\\g&h&i\end{pmatrix} \).
math_notes.mat_inv_3x3: The 3x3 matrix inverse via the adjugate (matrix of cofactors, transposed) divided by `mat_det_3x3`'s determinant -- the direct closed-form generalization of `mat_inv_2x2`, still undefined when singular.
math_notes.mat_det_n: The general \( n \times n \) determinant, computed as the product of `lu_factor`'s diagonal pivots (with a sign flip per row swap performed during pivoting) rather than cofactor expansion -- cofactor expansion is \( O(n!) \); LU-based determinant is \( O(n^3) \), the same cost as the factorization itself.
math_notes.mat_inv_n: The general \( n \times n \) matrix inverse, computed by solving \( AX = I \) column-by-column (each column of the identity matrix is a right-hand side for `mat_solve`) -- \( n \) linear solves rather than a closed-form adjugate formula, which is only practical at the 2x2/3x3 scale `mat_inv_2x2`/`mat_inv_3x3` target.
math_notes.mat_solve: Solves the linear system \( Ax = b \) for \( x \), via LU decomposition with partial pivoting (`lu_factor` then `lu_solve`) rather than computing \( A^{-1} \) explicitly and multiplying -- the standard, numerically preferred way to solve a single linear system.
math_notes.lu_factor: LU decomposition with partial pivoting: \( PA = LU \), where \( L \) is unit-lower-triangular (1s on the diagonal, implicit -- not stored), \( U \) is upper-triangular, and \( P \) is a row-permutation recorded as pivot indices (not a full permutation matrix) -- packed into one `Vec<f64>` per the README's packing convention.
math_notes.lu_det: \( \det A = \pm\prod_{i=1}^n U_{ii} \) -- the product of \( U \)'s diagonal entries from the packed LU factorization, with the sign flipped once per row swap `lu_factor` performed (tracked via the pivot record), since each row swap flips the determinant's sign.
math_notes.lu_solve: Given \( PA=LU \) (from `lu_factor`) and the same permutation applied to \( b \), solves \( Ax=b \) in two triangular passes: forward substitution \( Ly=Pb \), then back substitution \( Ux=y \) -- each \( O(n^2) \), far cheaper than the \( O(n^3) \) factorization itself, which is the whole point of factoring once and solving against multiple right-hand sides cheaply.
math_notes.cholesky_factor: For a symmetric positive-definite \( A \): \( A = LL^T \), where \( L \) is lower-triangular -- roughly half the work of general LU factorization by exploiting symmetry, but only valid when \( A \) is genuinely positive-definite (fails, rather than silently producing garbage, if a diagonal pivot ever comes out non-positive during factorization).
math_notes.cholesky_solve: Given \( A=LL^T \) (from `cholesky_factor`), solves \( Ax=b \) via forward substitution \( Ly=b \) then back substitution \( L^Tx=y \) -- the Cholesky analog of `lu_solve`.
math_notes.mat_eig_power: The power iteration method for the DOMINANT eigenvalue/eigenvector: repeatedly apply \( v_{k+1} = Av_k / \lVert Av_k \rVert \) starting from an arbitrary vector; \( v_k \) converges to the eigenvector of the eigenvalue with largest absolute value (assuming one exists and is unique), and the Rayleigh quotient \( v_k^T A v_k \) converges to that eigenvalue. Converges to a REAL eigenvalue only -- has no mechanism to detect a complex-conjugate dominant pair (see [vani-algebra](https://github.com/enthusiasticgeek/vani-algebra)'s README for how this limits its own root-finder built on top of this function).
math_notes.mat_eig_deflate: Given a found eigenpair \( (\lambda, v) \) (unit \( v \)), returns \( A - \lambda v v^T \) -- removes \( \lambda \)'s contribution so a second call to `mat_eig_power` on the result converges to the NEXT-largest eigenvalue instead of re-finding the same one. Requires \( A \) symmetric with orthonormal eigenvectors for this rank-1 deflation to be valid -- see [vani-algebra](https://github.com/enthusiasticgeek/vani-algebra)'s README for why its companion-matrix use case deliberately does NOT use this (a companion matrix isn't symmetric, so this trick would silently corrupt every root after the first).
math_notes.mat_cond: The 2-norm condition number \( \kappa(A) = \lambda_{\max}/\lambda_{\min} \) (ratio of the largest to smallest eigenvalue magnitude, via repeated `mat_eig_power`/`mat_eig_deflate`) -- large \( \kappa(A) \) means `mat_solve`'s answer is highly sensitive to small perturbations in \( A \) or \( b \); returns `f64_inf()` for a (numerically) singular matrix.
math_notes.mat_qr_householder: QR decomposition via Householder reflections: \( A = QR \), where \( Q \) is orthogonal (\( Q^TQ=I \)) and \( R \) is upper-triangular -- each Householder reflection zeroes out the entries below one diagonal pivot, applied successively.
math_notes.mat_svd_bidiag: The bidiagonalization step toward a full SVD: \( A = UBV^T \) where \( U,V \) are orthogonal and \( B \) is bidiagonal (nonzero only on the main diagonal and the superdiagonal) -- NOT a full SVD (diagonalizing \( B \) further needs an iterative implicit-shift QR sweep, out of this package's v0.2.0 scope per the README).
